evidence: The constructor receives OrderRepository and ProductRepository, which are domain interfaces, so there is no concrete persistence code.
changeState calls order.advanceTo(state) and cancelOrder calls order.cancel(), so the state-transition rules stay in the domain.
placeOrder loads products, calls products[index].reserve(...), then saves the products and the order: this is use-case orchestration.
toOrderView and toProductView map entities to the OrderView and ProductView data objects returned to callers.

Borderline: ensureStockIsAvailable adds up the requested quantity per product and throws DomainError on insufficient stock. A domain service could own this check, but it is acceptable as a pre-check in an application service.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: OrderService in src/application/order-service.ts does what an application layer should: it coordinates use cases. It reaches storage only through the domain repository interfaces passed into its constructor. State changes are left to the domain entities (advanceTo, cancel, reserve, release). It maps entities to view objects. It contains no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework code. The only borderline case is ensureStockIsAvailable, which adds up the quantity requested per product across an order's lines and throws DomainError when stock is too low. That is a check across several products before reserving, which is common in application services, and the product entity still does the reserving. The rubric's examples of failures are business rules in infrastructure or presentation files and infrastructure code in domain files, so this is not a clear violation.
